reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-four home runs in a full season from a 23-year-old third baseman is the kind of projection that needs the contact profile to hold it up, and Caminero's does. His 92.9 mph average exit velocity sits at the 95th percentile, his 50.5% hard-hit rate tells the same story from a different angle, and an xSLG of .496 says the raw power is already translating against big-league pitching. The discipline reads fine, an 11.5% walk rate well above average and a K% of 18.4% that doesn't bite, though the chase rate at 30.2% is the one thing worth watching as pitchers probe the outer half with experience against him. If the zone management holds, a .898 OPS projection off a .364 xwOBA is a fair landing spot; if pitchers find the weakness and the chase rate climbs, the power stays but the average and on-base drift, and you're looking at a thumper with some swing-and-miss cost rather than a complete offensive third baseman.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .399 xwOBA at the plate and a 2.72 xERA on the mound aren't two players — they're the same guy, and both numbers sit at the 95th percentile or better against their respective populations. The contact profile has a wrinkle: a 31.5% whiff rate keeps the strikeout number elevated at 24.2%, but a 15.8% barrel rate and 93.2 mph average exit velocity mean the damage when he connects is severe enough that pitchers have no clean way out. On the mound, a 30.4% whiff rate and a 3.8% barrel rate allowed describe a starter who misses bats and suppresses hard contact without needing elite command to do it. The projection's .906 OPS and 35 home runs are what you get when both sides of the profile hold, and right now both sides are holding.

His 50.5% hard-hit rate and 92.2 mph average exit velocity aren't soft-contact flukes dressed up in good luck — contact quality at that level sustains itself across a full season. reports.name: Sal Stewart

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: Wood's contact quality is about as good as it gets: 95.3 mph average exit velocity and a 20.5% barrel rate both sit at the 100th percentile, and a 16.8% walk rate means pitchers can't just work around the damage. The problem living inside this elite profile is a 28.3% strikeout rate that belongs to a replacement-level bat, not a .576 xSLG monster, and whether those two things can coexist at scale is the only question that matters. If the strikeouts stabilize anywhere near where the walk rate and 21.8% chase rate suggest they should, the projection's .912 OPS and 33 home runs are a floor, not a ceiling. If they don't, you still have an unusual producer profile, brutal to put away and brutal when he makes contact, just with enough empty at-bats to keep him from being truly great.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: The .403 OBP across AA & A+ & A, at 18 years old, is the whole argument. Willits has drawn 94 walks in 527 plate appearances this season, a walk rate that translates to 12.8% at the MLB level, well clear of the 8.5% MLB average, and the power, while still filling out, already produces a .193 ISO across those same levels. Sixty stolen bases tell you the profile isn't waiting around for the bat to catch up. The translation does bump his strikeout rate above league average, so the floor hinges entirely on whether that contact improves as he rises, but an 18-year-old shortstop holding a .855 OPS across three levels is either an everyday regular or a very good problem to have.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.published_report:
The xBA sits at 93rd percentile; the BB% sits at 2nd. That gap is the whole profile.

reports.published_report: The case for Perdomo is built almost entirely on plate discipline, and the Statcast profile makes it hard to argue. The problem is the power: a 2.7% barrel rate and 87.4 mph average exit velocity are both bottom-of-the-barrel Statcast figures, and the .344 xSLG reflects that honestly. What you get if it holds is a .359 OBP shortstop with 22 projected steals and elite defense by OAA, a profile that ages gracefully even if the bat never grows; what you lose if the discipline erodes, even slightly, is the whole argument, because there's no power floor to catch the fall.

reports.name: Sandy Alcantara
reports.published_report: The profile is built on contact suppression, not swing-and-miss. Alcantara's 97.4 mph fastball generates elite carry, his barrel rate sits at 5.6%, and he issues walks at a 6.6% clip that puts him in the top fifth of the league — but the 17.2% strikeout rate and 21.0% whiff rate expose the tradeoff: when he doesn't get soft contact, he has to strand traffic instead of ending innings. A 3.82 ERA over a projected 219.0 innings works if the ground balls and weak contact keep coming; a stretch where hitters square him up more consistently turns a mid-rotation workhorse into someone leaking runs faster than the peripherals suggest. The xERA of 3.90 and xwOBA of .305 say he's pitching about as well as his results, so there's no hidden debt owed, just the ongoing wager that contact management at a low-strikeout rate can carry a full workload.

At AAA in 2026, Williams has drawn 47 walks across 359 plate appearances, a 13% clip that maps to 10.8% in an MLB context, still above a league that walks at 8.5%, but his strikeout rate translates to 23.1% against that same league's 22.0%, and his ISO lands at .131 against a .15 MLB average, meaning the discipline shows up in the numbers but the power isn't carrying its weight once the level adjusts. The whole profile hinges on whether the batting average, currently sitting at .233 AAA with a .282 BABIP, can stabilize enough at the big-league level to keep the OBP functional without the power to compensate when it doesn't. Either a fringy everyday regular if the contact improves, or a bench bat whose walks keep him employed.

reports.name: Theo Gillen
reports.published_report: The .422 OBP and 44 stolen bases across AA & A+ are doing a lot of work for a 20-year-old, and the question isn't whether Theo Gillen can play, it's whether enough of this translates to carry a big-league roster spot. The raw line is loud: .315/.422/.550 in 525 PA, with 74 walks against 115 strikeouts, and the translation puts his BB% at 11.0 where MLB hitters average 8.5, so the plate discipline isn't a minor-league mirage. The ISO translates to .164, right at the MLB mean, which means the 22 home runs at these levels don't arrive as a slugger's profile on the other side. Everything hinges on the BABIP, .384 across AA & A+, and a left-handed contact hitter with elite speed who falls back to average on contact in center field looks like a useful bench piece; one who sustains contact quality becomes a low-end everyday player.

reports.name: Justin Crawford
reports.published_report: The sprint speed is elite, the power is near-absent, and those two facts are the whole tension in this profile. Crawford's 29.5 ft/s sits at the 96th percentile, and he makes contact well enough, with an 18.4% whiff rate, to put that speed to use on the basepaths and in the field. The problem is a 1.3% barrel rate and an xSLG of .316 that sits at the 3rd percentile, which means pitchers can attack the zone without real consequence, and a 37.7% chase rate suggests they're already finding that out. The floor if the hit tool softens further is a bench role where the speed remains the only leverage.

reports.name: Davis Martin
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells you almost everything you need to know: a 4.70 xERA with a 44.5% hard-hit rate and average exit velocity of 90.3 mph against him. Martin misses bats often enough to hold a roster spot, with a 32.2% chase rate and 7.3% walk rate that keep him from beating himself, but hitters make loud contact when they connect, and 2411 rpm on the fastball hasn't changed that. The projection at 4.08 ERA over 154.6 innings is friendlier than his underlying contact profile suggests it should be, so the whole thing hinges on whether the White Sox defense and sequencing luck hold to let him outrun that xERA gap. He's a back-end starter who works at the margins of strike-throwing, and if the contact quality stays where it is, the floor is a fifth starter who gives up more damage than the ERA says.

Across A+ & A, Miguel Sime Jr. is punching out batters at 16.2 per nine innings, 99th percentile in his pitcher pool, while issuing 8.0 per nine, a 9th-percentile control mark that translates to 7.1 walks per nine in MLB terms when the league sits around 3.2. The 130 strikeouts across 72.3 innings are backed by a sample large enough to trust the shape, but the 64 walks mean everything hinges on whether he can bring the zone into sharper focus as he climbs, because if the command doesn't move, a depth arm is the ceiling and the floor both.

Fifty-seven walks across 79.3 innings at A-ball translates to a 6.4 BB/9 at the MLB level, against a translation average of 3.2, and the K-BB% of 7 sits at the 21st percentile in the pitcher pool. reports.name: Nelson Rada
reports.published_report: Thirty-six stolen bases at AAA is loud. Everything else is quiet. At 20 years old, Nelson Rada is posting a .263/.363/.344 line across 542 plate appearances at the level, and the shape of it tells you exactly what he is: a disciplined, contact-oriented center fielder with almost no power, an ISO that translates to .088 at the MLB level while the average big-leaguer sits at .150. The walk rate translates favorably too, and 102 strikeouts in 542 PA is genuinely clean contact behavior for his age, but the profile hinges entirely on whether those 36 steals and the on-base skills can carry a lineup spot without the bat ever developing thump. If the power doesn't come, he's a bench piece or organizational depth, full stop.

reports.name: Xavier Isaac
reports.published_report: The power and the plate discipline are both loud, and the strikeout rate is the reason this profile has a ceiling problem. Across AAA & AA in 473 plate appearances, Isaac is walking at a 19% clip with 27 home runs and an .404 OBP, numbers that translate to a 14.1% walk rate and .186 ISO against big-league pitching — both comfortably above average. The strikeouts translated land at 29.3%, well past the 22.0% MLB mean, and at first base that's a narrowing filter: if he can't tighten the swing-and-miss against sharper stuff, the power and patience profile shrinks into a platoon piece rather than an everyday corner. Either a solid second-division regular or a left-handed bench bat who earns roster time in the right lineup construction.

reports.name: Mason Montgomery
reports.published_report: 102 strikeouts projected across 67.4 innings is the whole argument for Montgomery, and the Statcast current numbers back up every bit of it. His 38.2% strikeout rate sits at the very top of the league, his xERA is 2.56, and hitters are making weak enough contact that his .249 xwOBA translates to genuine run-prevention rather than smoke. The one live wire is the 9.3% walk rate, which is middling and the thing that keeps the projection at 2.86 ERA rather than something scarier, because when he misses the zone he misses it enough to let lineups breathe. If he tightens command even modestly, he's a shutdown late-inning arm with closer upside; if the walks persist, he's still a high-leverage weapon, just a slightly spiky one.

reports.name: Braylon Doughty
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. Across AA & A+, Doughty has issued just 25 walks in 104.4 innings, a 2.2 BB/9 that translates to 2.7 in MLB terms, comfortably under the MLB average of 3.2. That kind of command at 20 is the thing you can't teach, and the 1.3 WHIP says it's showing up in results. The strikeout side is more modest, 114 punchouts across AA & A+ translating to a 7.9 K/9 where the average MLB starter sits at 8.6, so this isn't a swing-and-miss profile riding a hot stretch, which is exactly why the ceiling lands at multi-inning reliever or setup role rather than something grander. If the command holds as he climbs, he's a useful late-inning weapon; if the stuff doesn't gain enough to bump that K rate, the floor is a depth arm who misses bats just often enough to stay on a roster.

reports.name: Connor Prielipp
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the one thing worth leaning on here: 24.8 K% puts him in the upper third of the league at missing bats, and the 95.6 mph fastball explains how he gets there. Everything else in the Statcast profile is ordinary to quietly concerning, and the 42.1% hard-hit rate is the one that does real damage — hitters who connect against him connect hard, which is why the xERA sits at 4.12 even when the strikeouts are working. The projection's 5.07 ERA over 122.4 innings reflects what happens when command slips even slightly on a profile that has no margin: 8.6 BB% is already a liability, and if he can't keep the fastball off the barrel more consistently, he's a back-end starter who gives up too many big innings to stay in a rotation.

reports.name: Sebastian Walcott
reports.published_report: The numbers are loud: .321/.399/.607 at AA in just 158 plate appearances after coming back from a UCL injury that wiped out his season start, with 9 home runs and an ISO of .286 that translates to .180 against MLB pitching. That translated ISO clears the MLB average, and his translated walk rate lands at 8.9% where the league sits around 8.5%, so the bat control isn't just a BABIP mirage at .383. The whole read hinges on the defensive profile — he's listed exclusively at DH at 20 years old, which means if the bat cools or the power doesn't carry, there's no glove to fall back on, and the floor drops to bench depth fast. Right now the production is hard to ignore, but a DH-only ceiling at this age either becomes a legitimate middle-of-the-order run producer or an organizational afterthought, and 158 PA after an injury return is just enough to raise the question without answering it.

reports.name: Heriberto Hernández
reports.published_report: The power is loud and the contact is the problem. A 14.1% barrel rate and .494 xSLG both sit in the 92nd percentile, and an xwOBA of .357 reflects contact quality that the raw line can't fully capture — but a 33.2% whiff rate at the 7th percentile bleeds enough of that value away to land the projected AVG at .226. The profile hinges on whether he can trim the whiff rate enough to let 91.5 mph average exit velocity translate into something closer to his .248 xBA; if he can't, the 26 projected home runs come packaged with cold stretches long enough to cost him at-bats. A streaky, boom-or-bust corner outfielder whose ceiling is a .767 OPS everyday player and whose floor is a platoon bat on a short leash.

He makes contact, a 14.5% strikeout rate is genuinely good, but the contact itself is soft, and a 38.4% chase rate explains why the walk rate sits at 6.9%, well below where it would need to be to compensate. The projection's .248/.304/.408 line with 23 home runs reads as a player whose counting stats are propped up by Atlanta's lineup and 692 plate appearances, not by underlying quality. At 29, at a premium defensive position he handles adequately, he's a regular by opportunity more than by profile.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries this profile. At 13.1% with a chase rate of 22.3%, Suzuki lives in the zone on his terms, and the .340 xwOBA reflects it even as the average exit velocity and hard-hit rate sit well below average. He barrels the ball at a 10.4% clip, which is what converts selective plate appearances into real power rather than empty contact, and the projection lands at 27 home runs with a .365 OBP across 639 plate appearances. The gap between his xBA (.246) and xSLG (.425) is wide enough to tell you this isn't a line-drive accumulator: he hits the ball hard when he hits it, he just doesn't hit it hard often. If the strikeout rate climbs and the elite chase discipline softens with age, the power thins and you're left with a passable average and diminishing run production; hold the discipline, and the .838 OPS projection looks conservative.

reports.name: Bryce Elder
reports.published_report: The xERA of 4.11 and the xwOBA of .313 land right at the median, which is about as honest a portrait as Statcast paints. Elder survives on contact management, not swing-and-miss: a 19.1% strikeout rate and a 21.6% whiff rate both sit well below average, and hitters aren't chasing at 27.6%. The barrel rate of 6.8% and the hard-hit rate of 39.9% tell a quieter story about how he gets by, keeping barrels down even when the fastball at 92.4 mph doesn't generate much deception. The whole profile hinges on sustaining that contact suppression, because if the barrel rate normalizes upward, there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him — just a back-end innings-eater trending toward the rotation's edge.

reports.name: Alex Bregman

reports.name: Herick Hernandez
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud and the walk rate is louder. Across AAA, AA, and A this season, Hernandez has 96 strikeouts in 74.7 innings, an 11.6 K/9 that translates to 9.3 at the MLB level, but the 6.4 BB/9 translates to 5.5, nearly double what a typical big-league arm gives away. That gap is the whole profile: the stuff misses bats, but a 53rd-percentile K-BB% says the strikeouts aren't outrunning the control problem by nearly enough. If the walk rate doesn't tighten, you're looking at a reliever or depth piece; if it does, there's a back-end starter in there somewhere, but the evidence strength is rated low and the sample doesn't yet say which way this tips.

reports.name: Justin Wrobleski
reports.published_report: The 3.85 ERA projection asks you to believe in a pitcher whose actual contact profile is ugly, and that's a real tension. His 5.5% walk rate is genuinely elite, but hitters are barreling him up at 9.8% and posting a 43.7% hard-hit rate against him, and his xERA sits at 4.73 with a .333 xwOBA behind it. The walk suppression keeps innings alive and limits damage on the margins, which is why 139.2 projected innings and a 1.16 WHIP are plausible outcomes even with the contact quality working against him. If the 31.8% chase rate holds and he keeps the ball in the yard more consistently, the gap between ERA and xERA closes; if hitters stop expanding and start squaring him up at that same rate, you're looking at a back-end innings-eater who gives the Dodgers length without giving them safety.

reports.name: Eric Hartman
reports.published_report: The 54 stolen bases are loud, and they should be, but the rest of the profile asks a harder question. Across AA & A+, Hartman is hitting .253/.353/.465 with 26 home runs and a .212 ISO, which looks like a genuine power-speed package until the translation scrubs some of it off: the ISO lands at .147 at the MLB level, essentially where the average MLB hitter sits, and the strikeout rate climbs to 27.9% once you account for the level. The speed is probably the most durable piece here, because raw stolen-base volume at 20 years old tends to survive level jumps better than raw power does. If the bat-to-ball doesn't sharpen, what's left is a corner outfielder with fringe MLB power and a strikeout problem, which is a bench bat at best.

reports.name: Troy Melton
reports.published_report: The gap between a 3.68 xERA and a projected 2.67 ERA is where the interesting argument lives. Melton generates chase at 32.6% and limits barrels to 6.4%, which is how you survive a 20.0% strikeout rate that sits well below average — he's getting weak contact and keeping hitters from spitting on pitches outside the zone, rather than blowing anyone away. The 96.4 mph fastball gives him the raw ingredient to miss more bats, but his 24.1% whiff rate says he isn't converting that velocity yet, and if the chase rate erodes, the strikeout floor becomes a real liability for a starter projected to eat 126.4 innings. If the contact-management holds, he's a solid mid-rotation contributor; if it slips, what's left is a fringy arm with ordinary swing-and-miss.

Ford has drawn 45 walks against 65 strikeouts across 257 AAA plate appearances in 2026, and that 18% walk rate translates to 12.8% at the MLB level — genuine plate discipline at a position where patience alone buys roster value. The problem is everything else: a .223 average, four home runs, and an ISO of .112 at AAA that translates to .116 at the MLB level, well short of what catchers typically need to hold a lineup spot. If the eye stays and contact ticks up enough to leverage those walks into real OBP, he's a backup catcher with an unusually patient approach worth keeping; if the bat stalls where it is, the walks sustain a career without earning him a regular role.

reports.name: Alec Bohm
reports.published_report: Contact rate is the engine here, and it runs clean. A 16.9% whiff rate and 14.8% K% put Bohm in genuinely rare company for a corner infielder, and the 90.5 mph average exit velocity with 43.2% hard contact says he's hitting the ball well enough to back it up. The problem is he almost never walks, a 6.9% BB% that sits near the bottom of the league, so all that contact skill bottlenecks into a .309 OBP and a .700 OPS projection across 627 PA. If he ever learns to take a pitch he can handle without chasing, the xBA at .260 and xSLG at .409 suggest a meaningfully better hitter than his slash line shows; if he doesn't, you're looking at a second-division regular whose value lives entirely in run production at the middle of a good lineup.

reports.name: Kane Kepley
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Across AA & A+, Kepley has drawn 118 walks against just 86 strikeouts in 576 plate appearances, a 20% walk rate that translates to a 14.8% MLB-equivalent clip, roughly 74% above what a typical big leaguer posts. The .427 OBP and 66 stolen bases tell you what kind of player he is: a left-handed center fielder who gets on base relentlessly and makes the defense pay for it, even when the raw power (a .124 MLB-equivalent ISO, below average) isn't going to scare anyone. The ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat, and the floor is basically the same thing, so the question isn't whether he breaks out, it's whether that contact rate holds at the next level long enough for the on-base skills to carry him onto a big-league roster.

reports.name: Devin Taylor
reports.published_report: The .417 BABIP is doing a lot of the work here, and that's the whole conversation. Across AAA, AA, and A+ this season, Devin Taylor is hitting .315/.418/.501 over 612 plate appearances, numbers that look like a legitimate top prospect until you run them through the MLB translator: the contact rate softens to a 28.8% strikeout rate, and the ISO collapses from .186 to .139, which trails the average big-league hitter. The walk rate translates to 11.7%, which is genuinely above average, so if the plate discipline holds, he has a real skill underneath the gaudy surface line. But if the BABIP normalizes and the strikeouts stay where they are, what's left is a bench outfielder with a good eye.

reports.name: Santiago Suarez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. At AA, 21 walks across 126 innings translates to a 2.1 BB/9 in MLB-equivalent terms, well below the 3.2 mark most pitchers run at that level, and that gap is wide enough to carry a guy whose 99 strikeouts don't translate to missing bats up top — the MLB-equivalent K/9 comes out at 6.6, well short of the 8.6 average. The control is real enough to keep him viable, but the ceiling math doesn't clear the bar: even with pinpoint command, a pitcher who misses few bats and works toward the middle of the zone doesn't have the margin for error a backend starter needs. Suarez is a depth arm if it stays together, and a depth arm if something slips.

reports.name: Max Meyer
reports.published_report: The 2614 rpm fastball spin is the whole engine here. Meyer's whiff rate sits at 28.6% and his K% at 26.2%, both comfortably above average, driven by a fastball that does unusual things at 95.1 mph because of that spin. The Statcast contact profile is the complication: an 8.6% barrel rate and 42.0% hard-hit rate suggest that when hitters do make contact, they're squaring it up, which is why the xERA of 3.86 is a full point higher than the projected 2.69 ERA. That gap is the bet ValuCast is making, that the strikeout shape and a WHIP of 1.14 across 112.0 projected innings will keep enough damage off the board, and it probably holds if the control (8.9% BB%) doesn't slip further.

reports.name: Tanner Bibee
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is honest about what he is: a strike-thrower who doesn't miss enough bats. An 18.9% strikeout rate and a 27.5% chase rate are both well below league average, and that's the core of the problem — when hitters aren't expanding the zone and you're not blowing them past pitches at the zone's edge, contact becomes the plan, and contact at 89.0 mph average exit velocity is manageable but not dominant. The control is the one genuine carrying tool, a 7.4% walk rate that sits better than most starters, and with 187.3 projected innings it keeps him valuable as an innings absorber even when everything else is middling. If the chase rate climbs, there's a rotation piece here; if it doesn't, he's a back-end arm whose ERA lives and dies by how much the defense and sequencing bail out a 4.33 xERA.

At AAA in 2026, Romero's 3.2 BB/9 ranks in the 82nd percentile among his peers, and that control translates to roughly average at the MLB level — not a weapon, but not a liability either. The problem is everything around it: 102 strikeouts across 125.3 innings produces a K/9 of 7.3, which the MLB-equivalent translation puts at 7.1, well below what MLB starters typically generate, and a translated K-BB% of 9.7 against a pool where the average sits at 13.5. He misses bats at a 10th-percentile rate in his own pool, which means the control advantage has to carry a profile that doesn't generate enough swing-and-miss to survive when it slips. The ceiling here is a depth arm, the floor is a depth arm, and the shape of that is a guy who sticks around as long as the walk numbers hold.

reports.name: Drew Cavanaugh
reports.published_report: The .449 OBP across AAA & AA is doing a lot of work here, and the BABIP of .401 is doing most of the heavy lifting behind it. Cavanaugh has 35 walks against 55 strikeouts in 227 plate appearances, which translates to an 11.4% walk rate when moved to an MLB context, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. If the average regresses hard and the power stays modest, you're left with a patient backstop who can work counts at the margin, which is a bench catcher, not a regular.

reports.name: Ty Southisene
reports.published_report: The contact-and-patience combination is legitimately special; the power is the problem. Across A+ & A this season, Southisene is hitting .300 with a 12% strikeout rate and 47 walks in 368 plate appearances, a plate-discipline profile that translates to roughly a 17.8% K rate and 9.7% walk rate at the MLB level — both sitting comfortably below and above what big-league hitters typically post. The ISO of .080 across A+ & A is the wall everything runs into, and the MLB-equivalent translation lands at .087, less than two-thirds of what the average major leaguer produces for power. The 34 stolen bases add a real dimension, and if the contact and strike-zone feel hold as he climbs, there's a path to a useful table-setter, but without a power signal emerging by Double-A, this profile ends at a bench piece whose value lives entirely in the top of the lineup.

The MLB-equivalent translation puts his ISO at .133, a step below what an average big-league bat produces, so the gap-to-gap game isn't going to carry him; what keeps him relevant is the contact rate and the legs, a .266/.356 line in 364 AAA plate appearances built on 41 walks and a strikeout rate that translates just a tick above big-league norms. This profile hinges entirely on whether the speed plays at the next level, because if it doesn't, you're left with a below-average power bat and a walk rate that lands near the middle of the pack. Bench outfielder with a real path to a specific role if a team values defense and baserunning; organizational depth if they don't.

reports.name: Caleb Lomavita
reports.published_report: The ISO is the argument: .209 at AA in 347 plate appearances, translating to a .156 MLB-equivalent for a 23-year-old catcher. That's a meaningful number, and the sample, 347 PA at a level where power travels honestly, gives it weight. The problem is everything around it: a translated strikeout rate of 24.7% with walks that translate to just 7.9%, and a .311 OBP at AA that has no obvious path to improve when the contact rates follow him up. If the power translates and the hit tool firms up even slightly, he's a viable backup with a bat worth carrying; if the contact rates hold where they are, what's left is a catcher who can't get on base enough to matter off the bench.

reports.name: Khristian Curtis
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate translates — 11.3 K/9 across AAA & AA becomes a legitimate 9.2 against MLB hitters, and that part of the profile is fine. Forty-eight free passes in 86.3 innings is the whole argument against him: a BB/9 that lands at 4.6 at the MLB level against a league that sits at 3.2, and that gap is what drags an otherwise interesting arm down to a 4.9 ERA and a 1.4 WHIP. The K-BB% is 16% across AAA & AA, which translates to 12.5% in the majors, a shade under the 13.5% MLB mark, because the strikeouts alone can't outrun that volume of walks. The ceiling here is a depth arm, and so is the floor; what little movement there is depends entirely on whether the command tightens, because right now the stuff profiles fine and the control does not.

The power isn't there yet, a .11 ISO at A that translates to .089 in MLB-equivalent terms, and the strikeout rate translates to 28.8% at that same level. This entire profile hinges on whether the speed and plate discipline can carry him as a table-setter once he climbs levels where the walks don't come as freely, and if the bat doesn't develop beyond this, he's a bench piece whose legs keep him employed rather than a center fielder with a future role.
